title: Ascension Day

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rogation days: walking the edges, asking for the harvest. Your line was beating the bounds. Which boundary did you notice, and what did you do on the other side of it? Day one thousand forty.

A small group of friends is standing on a hill outside Jerusalem with their heads tipped back, staring at an empty sky. A moment ago Jesus was talking with them. Then he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. It's the stance of someone left on a platform after the train has gone, still looking at the spot where someone used to be. Then two men in white are standing beside them, and in the King James Bible they ask a fair question: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven?" The book of Acts sets this after forty days of Jesus appearing to his friends. Today, Ascension Day.

Acts begins by saying the risen Jesus was "seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God." That's where the feast's timing comes from. Then the scene on the hill: "while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight." A cloud, in the Bible, can be more than weather. It's how God's presence shows up and hides at once, over the mountain, over the tent in the desert. So the cloud here isn't saying he got lost in the sky. Christians say he went into God's presence. They say it in the old creeds too: he ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. Churches understand that in different ways, some picturing an upward journey, some hearing "up" as the only word we have for going into God. Either way, in the texts it isn't a goodbye. Look how Luke ends his Gospel. After Jesus parts from them, "they worshipped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy." Not grief. Joy. Which is odd, until you set it beside Matthew, who doesn't tell the Ascension at all and ends his Gospel with a promise instead: "lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world." The leaving and the promise belong together. Some Christians put it this way: at the Ascension, Jesus stops being in one place so that he can be with his friends everywhere. And then the angels' question does its work. Stop staring up. Go back to the city. There's a wait coming, and then a job. Ascension Day is the feast of looking up, and then getting on with it.

Here's the practice: look up, then get on with it. If you can, go to a window or step outside. Settle, and breathe. Look up for a while. Sky, ceiling, clouds, whatever's there. Let your shoulders drop. If you pray, you can hold Matthew's line in the quiet: lo, I am with you alway. If you don't, simply notice the size of the sky over your small day. Then, when the bell comes, bring your eyes down to the next ordinary thing in front of you, and start it. The bell holds the time.
Ascension Day. Forty days after Easter, the feast of Jesus taken up into God's presence, and the promise that he stays with his friends.
Your line: he is with you always. Today, each time you catch yourself staring at what's gone, look up once, then turn back to the next thing in front of you. Day one thousand forty.

howItsDone: Churches that keep Ascension Day mark it forty days after Easter with a service reading the end of Luke and the start of Acts; some move the celebration to the following Sunday.

Editor pass: hook no longer opens on a KJV quotation followed by 'That's X, in the King James Bible' (the same opener as 1032 and 1038, with 1045 next); it now opens on the scene, and 'anyone who has watched a train pull out knows that stance' (telling the listener what they know) became a plain image. The 'moment Jesus stops being in one place' summary is now attributed to 'some Christians' rather than to Christians generally.
Audit pass: the teach read as if Matthew's closing promise were part of the Ascension scene; it now says plainly that Matthew doesn't narrate the Ascension and the two endings are set side by side.
